images.text:
You might never be able to hit a golf ball like Tiger Woods, but according to expert David Diaz, there is at least one part of his technique that you can mimic: the posture.
“It's the most underrated part of the golf game,” says David. “Everybody wants to get out there and work on their swing, but nobody pays attention to the part that precedes the swing: the address.” The address is everything that happens before a golfer begins to move the club towards the ball. David insists that the address needs to be practiced as often as the swing does, so that it becomes a subconscious and repeatable action.

“Most golfers measure success in superlatives,” Diaz continues. “Longest drive, lowest score. What I try to do is emphasize another superlative: straightest back.”
“You've got a lot of moving parts in the swing,” states Diaz. “You've got to keep your shoulder blades flat, bend your knees a bit, maintain the proper spine angle, and then flex your trunk as you transfer your weight. And you have to make sure that all of these different parts cooperate in that one fluid and harmonic swing.”

Golf is a game of repetition. If the posture is incorrect, each swing and impact has a cumulative effect on your muscles and joints. Those who plan to be playing the game for years or decades to come need to show a little bit of foresight.
“The golfer that fails to practice disciplined posture can expect to face a myriad of discomforts down the road,” Diaz warns. “The most common ailments include hyperextended joints, strained obliques and pulled backs.”
“Everybody wants to spend their golden years walking the golf course,” concludes David. “But you can't very well walk the golf course if you can't walk.”

Prepositions are words that tell time, location or movement.
Prepositional prefixes are prefixes that are built on prepositions.

You put prefixes at the beginning of words in order to modify the original words.
Prepositional prefixes modify the original words in relation to time, position, size or movement.
Here are a few prepositional prefixes:

Stress in Words beginning in sub-, super-, hyper-, co-, and under-

In some words with prefixes, the prefix is stressed, like in supermarket.
In some words with prefixes, the main stress is on a syllable after the prefix, like supernatural.
You usually stress prepositional prefixes when they are part of a noun, like supernatural or hypertext. The main stress is on the prefix, and the secondary stress is later in the word.
However, when the words are adjectives, you usually stress the syllable after the prefix, like supernatural or hyperactive.
